caption:
Apple's Claris unit is testing Harbor, a Mac app that turns a Mac into a private AI server for open models.
Link several Thunderbolt 5 Macs and it pools their memory to run models too big for one machine.
It is a private preview for now, with no price or release date.

Would you run AI on your own Mac instead of the cloud?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

threads_text: Apple is quietly testing Harbor, a Mac app that runs open AI models right on your Mac and can chain several Macs together for bigger ones. No cloud, no per-token bill, at least on paper. Would you pay for a Mac just to run AI at home?

paragraphs.text: Claris, the Apple subsidiary best known for the FileMaker database software, is testing a Mac app called Harbor that runs open-weight AI models directly on a user's own computers, according to reports published on November 10 and 11, 2026. The app turns a Mac into a private inference server, so prompts and data stay on the user's hardware instead of being sent to a cloud provider.

The app first surfaced on November 10, when leaker Aaron Perris posted about it on X. 9to5Mac and MacRumors followed with reports the same day. Cult of Mac reported that Apple removed an App Store listing for Harbor after Perris found it, tbreak said in its summary of the coverage.

According to the reports, Harbor lets users browse, download and load open-weight models from inside the app, and it handles model management for them. The promotional copy quoted in the coverage promises setup with no manual configuration, no command line and no infrastructure expertise.

The feature that stands out is clustering. Two or more Macs with Thunderbolt 5 can be linked so that their unified memory works as one pool. The reports say this can be used to run models larger than a single Mac can hold, or to serve more requests at the same time. Harbor reportedly detects the connected machines and forms the cluster automatically.

Globe TV reported that the marketing copy describes the setup as having zero cloud fees and no per-token billing. MacRumors noted that Apple added support for RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 in macOS Tahoe 26.2, the networking feature that makes this kind of memory pooling practical.

Harbor is currently a private preview with early access sign-ups. Startup Fortune, citing MacRumors, reported that the sign-up page asks for company information, which suggests Claris is aiming first at businesses and developers rather than casual users. Apple has not commented, and no price or release date has been announced.

Tools for running models locally on Macs already exist. LM Studio and Ollama run models on a single machine, and the open-source Exo project can spread a model across several Macs. Startup Fortune noted that Ollama and LM Studio also run on Windows and Linux, while Harbor is built for Apple silicon only.

Coverage differed on timing. tbreak said 9to5Mac expects a public launch in the coming weeks or months, while AppleInsider said end users should not expect the app soon. None of the reports said which Mac models will support clustering.

For NeuraFeed, the notable part is who is building it. Running large open models across several Macs has so far been a hobbyist project that needs technical setup. A first-party app from an Apple subsidiary would turn the Mac Studio and Mac mini into an off-the-shelf option for companies that want AI without sending their data to an outside service, and it would give Apple a direct role in local AI beyond its own Apple Intelligence features.
The next signal is whether Claris publishes pricing and a supported hardware list, and whether Harbor opens to individual Mac owners or stays a business product.
